catalog_locator: Introduction, sec. 2 transcription notes, heading 'Tones', book p. 9 (p. 13, right half of the 2-up scan); Bele chapter sec. 7.1.2 'Tone classes', book pp. 19-20. Bele chapter = book pp. 17-31.
catalog_quote: Tones. These languages all have two phonemic tones only. An occasional fall, analyzable as high-low on one syllable, is indicated. Rising tones are also found, but all examples here are on word final long vowels. In these cases it is difficult to determine whether this is Cǐi (a single syllable with a rising tone) or Cìyí (two syllables with the last syllable beginning in a semi-vowel homorganic to the vowels). A downstep (lowered high after high) is also found. In no case was downstep found to play an important morpho-syntactic role. It nearly always was an obvious contraction of high-low-high to high-downstep. [Bele, sec. 7.1.2, pp. 19-20] Tone classes. All monosyllabic verbs have high tone. Verbs with the root shape CVC- are high if used as -u verbs, but note that the verb 'go out' mentioned at the end of the preceding paragraph is low if used as an -a verb (the same rule applies in Bo). CVCC- and CVVC- verbs all have low tone.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bele, like the other Bauchi-area Bole-Tangale languages Schuh sketches, is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with occasional HL falls, rises on final long vowels and phonetic downstep; verbs fall into lexical/shape-determined H vs L tone classes. The source says nothing about word stress or accent, for Bele or for the group.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: rising tones only on word-final long vowels (analysis Cǐi vs Cìyí left open); downstep non-functional.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level statement in the book's Introduction explicitly covering the eight languages sketched (Daza, Bele, Deno, Kubi, Kirfi, Galambu, Gera, Geruma); Bele chapter based on 1.5 h of elicitation with one speaker, tone marked on citation forms and short verb phrases. No stress statement exists in the only first-hand description.
new_statements.identity_note: Schuh's Bele data are from a single speaker (Mai Jagalwa Muhammadu) at Jagalwa village, ~50 miles east of Bauchi, 1.5 hours of elicitation on 15 April 1975; self-name Àɓéelé. This is the variety Glottolog registers as beel1236 (its subclassification comment cites this very book). The tone statement quoted is group-level (covers all eight Bauchi-area Bole-Tangale languages sketched, Bele included); the Bele chapter itself marks Hi/Lo tone throughout and gives Bele verb tone classes, but has no prosody paragraph of its own beyond segmental remarks.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent anywhere (0 hits in text; pp. 9 and 17 read as page scan). Introduction p. 9 'Tones': 'These languages all have two phonemic tones only' plus falls, rises on final long vowels, non-functional downstep. Bele chapter (pp. 17-31): 'Remarks on Phonology' covers only *s/*z > h and schwa; tone marked on all data; sec. 7.1.2 gives Bele verb tone classes (monosyllabic verbs H, CVVC-/CVCC- verbs L).
